title: WHY DID GOD LET MOSES DIE WHEN HIS BODY WAS STILL STRONG? THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD LET MOSES DIE WHEN HIS BODY WAS STILL STRONG? THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE

He was 120 years old. His eyes had not grown dim. His strength had not disappeared. He could still climb a mountain. But God told him his journey was over. What happened on that mountain reveals a terrifying truth about disobedience, an astonishing truth about grace, and a hope that reaches all the way to Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about the death of Moses.
Because Moses did not die the way we might expect a 120-year-old man to die.
His body had not collapsed under the weight of old age.
His eyesight had not failed.
His physical strength had not disappeared.
He was still capable of climbing a mountain.
Still able to see the land he had spent forty years leading an entire nation toward.
And yet...
He would never walk into it.
Imagine standing close enough to see the fulfillment of your life's greatest assignment, only to hear God tell you that someone else would finish the journey.
Imagine spending decades carrying people who complained about you, questioned your leadership, rebelled against your authority, and sometimes wished they had never followed you.
Imagine praying for those same people when God threatened judgment.
Imagine standing between a rebellious nation and the consequences of its sins.
And then imagine watching those people prepare to enter the land you had longed to see.
Without you.
This was not the death of a man whose body had finally given up.
This was the death of a servant whose earthly assignment had reached the boundary God had established.
And the reason behind that boundary is more serious than many of us realize.

Because hidden within the final moments of Moses is a warning about the holiness of God, the danger of misrepresenting Him, and the astonishing mercy of a Savior who can accomplish what even Moses could not.
But before we reach that mountain, we need to go back to a rock.
A rock in the wilderness.
A thirsty nation.
An exhausted leader.
And one moment of anger that changed everything.
The Bible records Moses' final moments in Deuteronomy 34:5–7:

"So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day. And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."
— Deuteronomy 34:5–7, King James Version
Read that final sentence again.
"His eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."
In Hebrew, the description is striking:
לֹא־כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ וְלֹא־נָס לֵחֹה
Lo-kahatah eino, ve-lo-nas lecho.
Literally, the passage describes Moses' eye as not having grown dim and his vitality as not having departed.

The Hebrew word לֵחֹה (lecho) is associated with freshness or vitality. It communicates that Moses had not suffered the ordinary depletion of physical vigor that we might expect at his extraordinary age.
Scripture is emphasizing something remarkable.
Moses was old in years, but he had not been physically reduced to helplessness.
And this matters because the text refuses to let us assume that Moses died simply because his body was worn out.
God had appointed the conclusion of his life.
But why?
Why would God bring such a faithful servant so close to the Promised Land and then refuse to let him enter?
Was Moses not the man who confronted Pharaoh?
Was he not the man through whom God brought the plagues upon Egypt?
Was he not the man who lifted his staff as the Red Sea opened?
Was he not the man who received the commandments on Mount Sinai?
Was he not the man who repeatedly interceded for Israel when the people turned against the Lord?
Yes.
He was all those things.
But he was also a man who needed God's mercy.
And one of the most dangerous assumptions a believer can make is that years of faithful service somehow make personal disobedience insignificant.
That is where this story begins to reach into our own hearts.
Because you can serve God publicly while struggling to surrender privately.
You can know Scripture and still allow anger to control your words.
You can be genuinely called by God and still make decisions that misrepresent His character.
You can do extraordinary things in His name and still need correction.
Moses knew what it meant to carry responsibility.
And responsibility can become exhausting.
The Israelites had complained again.
They were thirsty.
They were frustrated.
They accused Moses and Aaron of bringing them into a wilderness where there was no water.
And God gave Moses a specific instruction.
Numbers 20:8 records the Lord telling him to take the rod, gather the congregation, and speak to the rock before their eyes.
God promised that water would come forth.
Notice the instruction.
Speak.
Not strike.
Speak.
But something happened inside Moses.
The accumulated frustration of leadership erupted.
He gathered the people and said:
"Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?"
— Numbers 20:10, KJV
Then Moses lifted his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod.
Water came out.
The people drank.
Their animals drank.
The immediate crisis was resolved.
But Moses had disobeyed God.
And that is the uncomfortable part.
Water came out of the rock, but the presence of a miracle did not mean Moses' disobedience had God's approval.
Think about that.
Something visibly powerful happened.
The people received what they needed.
Yet God confronted the very leader through whom the miracle occurred.
This should humble anyone who serves in ministry.
Visible results are not always proof that every action, attitude, or decision behind them was right.
A congregation may be helped by a message even when the messenger needs repentance.
A family may receive blessings while a parent still needs to confront destructive anger.
A ministry may grow while its leaders still need correction.
God's faithfulness to His people must never be confused with His endorsement of everything done by His servants.
Then came the words that changed Moses' future.
"Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them."
— Numbers 20:12, KJV
The Hebrew phrase לֹא־הֶאֱמַנְתֶּם בִּי (lo-he'emantem bi) means, in context, "you did not believe in me" or "you did not trust me."
And the phrase לְהַקְדִּישֵׁנִי (lehaqdisheni) means "to sanctify me" or "to show me as holy."
God was not merely addressing the physical act of striking a rock.
He was addressing a failure of trust and a failure to uphold His holiness before the people.
Moses and Aaron had been entrusted with representing God.
But in that moment, Moses' anger and disobedience distorted that representation.
Psalm 106:32–33 also connects the incident with Moses speaking rashly after the people provoked him.
This was not an innocent misunderstanding.
Nor was it merely that Moses used the wrong technique to obtain water.
The Lord Himself explained the deeper issue.
They had failed to trust Him and honor Him as holy.
And because Moses was a leader, his actions carried enormous weight.
James 3:1 later reminds believers that teachers will receive stricter judgment.
Leadership is not a license to become careless with God's character.
It is a calling to greater faithfulness.
Perhaps you have never stood before a rock in the wilderness.
But have you ever been so angry that you spoke in a way that made someone question the God you claim to follow?
Have you ever used the truth of Scripture as a weapon against someone you were supposed to love?
Have you ever allowed your exhaustion to become an excuse for cruelty?
Have you ever insisted that your intentions were good while refusing to acknowledge that your actions were wrong?
That is why this story is so uncomfortable.
Because Moses' failure does not look entirely foreign to us.
It looks painfully human.
And if we are willing to be honest, we can recognize pieces of ourselves in his frustration.
We know what it feels like to carry responsibilities no one else seems to understand.
We know what it feels like to help people who do not appreciate the sacrifice.
We know what it feels like to pray, serve, forgive, and continue showing up while something inside us becomes increasingly tired.
Sometimes we are not angry because we stopped caring.
Sometimes we are angry because we have been carrying more than we know how to surrender.
But exhaustion does not turn disobedience into obedience.
Pain does not give us permission to misrepresent God.
And spiritual responsibility never removes our need for humility.
Moses was not exempt.
Neither are we.
Yet there is something equally important we must not overlook.
God's discipline did not mean that God had stopped loving Moses.
The Lord did not erase Moses from the story of redemption.
He did not declare that the decades of faithful service had been meaningless.
He did not withdraw every expression of His relationship with him.
In fact, the final chapter of Deuteronomy still calls Moses "the servant of the LORD."
The Hebrew expression is:
עֶבֶד־יְהוָה (eved-YHWH)
The servant of the LORD.
What a remarkable description to find in the account of a man who had experienced such a serious consequence for disobedience.
Moses was disciplined.
But he was still remembered as God's servant.
His sin had consequences.
But his entire life was not reduced to that failure.
And someone reading this needs to understand the difference.
There are consequences that repentance does not necessarily remove.
A broken trust may require years to rebuild.
A careless decision may permanently change a relationship.
A destructive habit may leave wounds that take time to heal.
A missed opportunity may never return in the same form.
God's forgiveness is real.
But forgiveness does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
And yet...
Consequences do not have to be the final word about your relationship with God.
That is not permission to minimize sin.
It is an invitation to take both holiness and grace seriously.
Because the God who disciplines His children is also the God who calls sinners to repentance and receives those who come to Him in faith.
And then we arrive at one of the most heartbreaking moments in Moses' life.
Deuteronomy 3:23–26 reveals that Moses pleaded with the Lord to let him cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan.
He wanted to enter.
After everything, he still wanted to finish the journey.
But the Lord told him:
"Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter."
— Deuteronomy 3:26, KJV
Imagine hearing those words.
Not from an enemy.
Not from a king.
Not from the people who had opposed you.
But from the God you had spent your life serving.
Moses had to accept an answer he did not want.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because sometimes the hardest act of faith is not believing that God can open a door.
Sometimes it is trusting Him when He tells you that a particular door will remain closed.
Some of us are still grieving the life we thought we would have.
The marriage we hoped would survive.
The relationship we wanted to repair.
The years we wish we could recover.
The calling we imagined would unfold differently.
The prayer we begged God to answer in one particular way.
We keep looking at the door.
We keep replaying the moment.
We keep wondering whether everything would have changed if we had done something differently.
And sometimes there really are things we must repent of.
Sometimes there are people we need to apologize to.
Sometimes there are consequences we must accept.
But even when God does not reverse a consequence, we are not abandoned to hopelessness.
His grace is greater than the boundary of one earthly opportunity.
Moses would not lead Israel across the Jordan.
Joshua would.
And that transition teaches another difficult lesson.
God's purposes are greater than any one servant, no matter how extraordinary that servant may be.
Moses was indispensable to the role God had assigned him, but God's covenant promises did not depend on Moses living forever.
The mission would continue.
The people would enter.
The promise would stand.
God remained faithful.
And Moses had to entrust the future to the Lord rather than insist on personally completing everything he had begun.
That is a lesson many of us resist.
We want to see every result.
We want to witness every breakthrough.
We want to know that our sacrifices were worth it.
We want to be present when the people we have prayed for finally change.
But sometimes we are called to plant what someone else will harvest.
Sometimes we are called to prepare a generation for a future we will not personally experience.
Sometimes faithfulness means releasing the work into God's hands.
And sometimes the greatest evidence of trust is accepting that God's story will continue without us at the center.
Then Moses climbed Mount Nebo.
Deuteronomy 34:1–4 records that the Lord showed him the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
There it was.
The land of promise.
The destination that had shaped decades of wilderness wandering.
He could see it.
But he would not enter it.
And there, in Moab, Moses died.
Scripture does not describe a prolonged illness.
It does not say his strength finally failed.
It does not tell us that his eyes closed because he had become too weak to continue.
It simply tells us that Moses died according to the word of the Lord.
There is an important Hebrew expression in Deuteronomy 34:5:
עַל־פִּי יְהוָה (al-pi YHWH)
Literally, "upon the mouth of the LORD," an idiom meaning "according to the command" or "at the word of the LORD."

Some Jewish interpretive traditions beautifully associate this wording with a death by divine kiss. That is a traditional interpretation, not an explicit statement that the biblical text describes God physically kissing Moses.
The text itself makes the central point clear.
Moses' death occurred according to God's word.
It was not presented as the unavoidable result of physical deterioration.
And Deuteronomy 34:6 adds another remarkable detail.
Moses was buried in the land of Moab, but the location of his grave remained unknown.
The passage attributes the burial to God, although interpreters differ over whether the Hebrew should be understood as the Lord Himself burying Moses or the burial occurring under His direction.
Either way, the narrative leaves us with a striking picture.
The great leader of Israel is gone.
His grave is unknown.
His body is not the center of Israel's worship.
His legacy is not preserved through a monument that people must visit.
The focus remains on the Lord who called him.
The Lord who sustained him.
The Lord who corrected him.
The Lord who fulfilled His promises.
But this is not where the story ends.
And what happens next changes the emotional weight of everything we have just read.
Because centuries later, Moses appears again in the biblical narrative.
Not as a forgotten failure.
Not as a man discarded by God.
But standing in glory beside Jesus Christ.
Matthew 17:1–3 records the Transfiguration.
Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain.
His appearance was transformed before them.
His face shone like the sun.
His clothing became white as light.
And suddenly, Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with Him.
Read that carefully.
Moses.
The man who had died outside the Promised Land.
The man who had pleaded to enter and had been denied.
The man whose earthly assignment had ended on Mount Nebo.
Now appeared with Christ in glory.
Luke 9:30–31 tells us that Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about His approaching departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
The Greek word used there is extraordinary.
ἔξοδος (exodos)
It means "departure" or "going out."
It is the same Greek word from which we get the English word exodus.
Consider the beauty of that connection.
Moses, whom God used to lead Israel out of slavery in Egypt, was now speaking with Jesus about the departure He would accomplish in Jerusalem.
The first exodus brought Israel out of Egypt.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus would accomplish the decisive saving work to which the Scriptures had been pointing.
Moses had led people through the wilderness.
Jesus would confront sin, death, and the powers of darkness through His cross and resurrection.
Moses had mediated the covenant given at Sinai.
Jesus would establish the new covenant in His blood.
Moses had led Israel toward an earthly inheritance.
Jesus would open the way to an eternal inheritance for those who belong to Him.
And there is another beautiful detail.
The Transfiguration took place in the land of Israel, although the Gospels do not identify the mountain with certainty.
So Moses, who had once been forbidden to cross into Canaan during his earthly ministry, is later seen in the land in the presence of the Messiah.
Scripture does not explicitly say that this appearance was God's delayed reward for Moses' earlier disappointment.
We should not claim more than the text reveals.
But we can say this with confidence.
Moses' exclusion from Canaan did not mean his exclusion from the glory of Christ.
That distinction is breathtaking.
His earthly discipline was real.
His failure was serious.
His death was final as far as his earthly leadership was concerned.
But his story in Scripture was not reduced to the worst moment of his life.
And there is hope here for every believer who has ever looked back on a mistake and wondered whether God could still receive them.
Because the Gospel does not teach that sin is harmless.
It teaches that sin is so serious that the Son of God gave Himself to save sinners.
And grace is so powerful that those who come to Christ in repentance and faith can be forgiven, cleansed, and reconciled to God.
Moses was a great servant.
But Moses was not the Savior.
That is the heart of the matter.
Hebrews 3:5–6 describes Moses as faithful in God's house as a servant, while Christ is faithful over God's house as the Son.
Moses could lead Israel out of Egypt.
But he could not remove the guilt of sin from the human heart.
Moses could deliver the law.
But he could not give himself as the final sacrifice for the sins of the world.
Moses could intercede for Israel.
But he could not accomplish the perfect redemption that Jesus would secure.
Moses could point toward the promise.
But only Jesus is the fulfillment of God's saving purposes.
And this is why the death of Moses must ultimately lead us to the cross of Christ.
Because if the story ends with Moses on Mount Nebo, we are left primarily with the sorrow of a faithful but imperfect servant who suffered a severe consequence.
But when we read Moses in light of Jesus, we see something much greater.
We see the limits of human righteousness.
We see the seriousness of God's holiness.
We see the need for a greater Mediator.
And we see the Son of God who perfectly obeyed the Father.
Where Moses failed to honor God rightly in a decisive moment, Jesus remained obedient even unto death.
Where Moses could not bring the people into the land, Jesus brings His people into the salvation and rest that only He can give.
Where Moses' ministry ended in death, Jesus rose from the dead.
The contrast is not meant to humiliate Moses.
It is meant to exalt Christ.
Because even the greatest heroes of the Bible are not the ultimate heroes of the Bible.
Jesus is.
And perhaps that is the deepest lesson of all.
You can admire Moses.
You can learn from his courage.
You can be strengthened by his endurance.
You can be warned by his disobedience.
But you must never place your hope in becoming so strong, so disciplined, or so religious that you no longer need a Savior.
You need Jesus.
Not merely as an example.
Not merely as a source of motivation.
Not merely as someone who helps you feel better about your past.
You need Him as Redeemer.
As Lord.
As the One who bore sin and conquered death.
As the One who calls you to turn from sin and trust Him.
As the One who gives grace that cannot be earned by decades of religious achievement.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
Grace is not the reward for being impressive.
It is God's gift to the undeserving through Jesus Christ.
And that is why no one is beyond the need for repentance.
Not the pastor.
Not the preacher.
Not the ministry leader.
Not the person who has served God for fifty years.
Not the believer who knows every familiar verse.
Not the person who has led others to Christ.
We all stand in need of the mercy of God.
And the good news is that Christ is sufficient.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying the shame of something you did years ago.
You have replayed it so many times that the memory has become part of how you see yourself.
You know God forgives.
You have told other people that God forgives.
But when it comes to your own story, you still struggle to believe that grace can reach that far.
Or perhaps you are living with a consequence that has not disappeared.
You repented.
You asked forgiveness.
You tried to make things right.
But the relationship remains broken.
The opportunity is gone.
The consequences remain.
And sometimes you wonder whether God is still willing to use someone like you.
Look at Moses.
Do not minimize his sin.
Do not pretend the consequences were imaginary.
But do not overlook the fact that Scripture still honors him as the servant of the Lord and later shows him with Christ in glory.
Your failures may have consequences.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your failures do not have authority to cancel His promise of eternal life.
Romans 8:1 says:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
That is not permission to keep living in rebellion.
It is freedom from condemnation for those who are in Christ.
Grace does not teach us to become comfortable with sin.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
True grace changes us.
It humbles us.
It teaches us to confess.
It moves us toward obedience.
It restores our worship.
It makes us grateful for a Savior we could never deserve.
And maybe today, the most important question is not why Moses died while he was still strong.
Maybe the question is why we keep postponing surrender while we are still alive.
We assume we have more time.
More opportunities.
More years to apologize.
More chances to forgive.
More mornings to repent.
More Sundays to take our faith seriously.
We tell ourselves that one day we will stop hiding.
One day we will stop compromising.
One day we will seek Christ with our whole heart.
But Moses' final chapter reminds us that physical strength is not a guarantee of tomorrow.
You can feel healthy and still be mortal.
You can have plans and still not control the length of your life.
You can be full of ambition and still be accountable to the God who gave you breath.
Psalm 90, traditionally attributed to Moses, contains this prayer:
"So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
— Psalm 90:12, KJV
What an extraordinary prayer when read alongside Moses' final days.
Teach us to number our days.
Not to fear every moment.
Not to live in constant panic.
But to live wisely.
To stop treating repentance as something that can always wait.
To stop postponing reconciliation.
To stop measuring our lives only by achievement.
To stop confusing outward success with inward faithfulness.
To remember that the most important thing about our lives is not how long we live, how much we accomplish, or how many people remember our names.
It is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
And whether we are walking faithfully with Him today.
There may be someone reading this who has been hiding behind a Christian appearance for years.
You know how to say the right words.
You know when to raise your hands in worship.
You know how to encourage someone else.
But privately, your heart has become distant.
Your prayer life has become mechanical.
Your compromises have become normal.
Your love for Christ has grown cold.
And the most dangerous part is that you have learned how to appear spiritually healthy while slowly neglecting your soul.
Moses was physically strong at 120.
But the condition of a person's body cannot tell us everything about their standing before God.
So examine your heart.
Not with despair.
Not with the belief that one mistake has placed you beyond God's reach.
But with the seriousness of someone who understands that eternity matters.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have been running from God, turn back.
If you have wounded someone, seek to make it right where possible.
If you have placed your confidence in religious accomplishments, surrender that false security.
If you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ, come to Him.
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy enough to purchase the grace of God.
Come because Jesus is worthy.
Come because He died for sinners.
Come because He rose again.
Come because His mercy is greater than anything you could earn.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to perform a public confession to prove that your repentance is sincere.
God sees the heart.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to earn forgiveness.
But to remind another struggling soul that they are not alone in seeking the Lord.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus met you in the aftermath of your own mistakes, consider sharing it. Your story may encourage someone who believes their life is already beyond restoration.
That is why these biblical truths matter so much.
Every day, people are scrolling through messages that teach them to chase success, defend their pride, celebrate their desires, and build their identities around temporary things.
But souls need something deeper.
They need the truth of Scripture.
They need the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
They need to understand both the holiness of God and the mercy of God.
They need discipleship that goes beyond an emotional moment.
They need encouragement that does not compromise biblical truth.
They need a faith that can survive disappointment, correction, suffering, and the ordinary struggles of life.
This is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not to build admiration around a human name.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell God's favor.
But to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ, His Word, and the life of repentance, faith, and obedience to which He calls us.
And if these messages have strengthened your walk with Christ, there is a meaningful way you can help us continue and expand this work.
It helps sustain the time, effort, and resources involved in this ministry.
It is a practical way to participate in the work of making biblical truth more accessible.
Your local church deserves faithful prayer, participation, and financial stewardship according to biblical conviction.
Because the goal is not to pressure anyone into giving.
The goal is to invite those who believe in this mission to help carry it forward.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
It is participating in a mission that seeks to keep Jesus Christ at the center.
These free resources are part of the desire to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and develop a more mature walk with the Lord.
But because someone in your circle may be quietly struggling with regret, exhaustion, or the fear that their failures have made them useless to God.
You may never know who reads it.
You may never hear their story.
But you can help place a Scripture-centered message where someone might encounter it at the very moment they need encouragement to turn to Christ.
Not everyone will agree with every message.
Not everyone will be ready to receive it.
But everyone deserves to hear the truth about Jesus Christ with clarity, humility, and love.
Christ alone is the foundation of our salvation.
And now, before you leave, return with me to Mount Nebo one last time.
An old man stands at the edge of a promise.
His eyes are clear.
His strength remains.
The land stretches before him.
He has led a nation through the wilderness.
He has seen the power of God.
He has known the burden of leadership.
He has experienced extraordinary intimacy with the Lord.
He has also experienced the consequences of his own disobedience.
And now his earthly journey is ending.
No triumphant procession into Canaan.
No final celebration as the leader of the conquering nation.
No monument marking the location of his grave.
Just a servant.
A mountain.
A promise he can see but cannot enter.
And the God whose faithfulness is greater than any human life.
But centuries later, on another mountain, Moses stands with Jesus.
And there, the story points us toward a truth far greater than the tragedy of an unfinished earthly assignment.
God's redemptive plan was never ultimately about Moses entering Canaan.
It was about the Savior who would come.
The Savior who would fulfill the law.
The Savior who would bear the judgment that sinners deserve.
The Savior who would rise from the dead.
The Savior who would call people from every nation to repentance and faith.
The Savior who would give His people an inheritance that death itself cannot take away.
And that Savior is Jesus Christ.
So if you have been standing at the edge of your own disappointment, remember Moses.
If you have been excusing your disobedience because of your past service, remember Moses.
If you have been confusing outward strength with spiritual security, remember Moses.
If you have been believing that your worst failure must be the final chapter of your life, remember what Scripture reveals about Moses standing with Christ.
And above all...
Look to Jesus.
Because the answer to your deepest need is not another chance to prove that you are strong enough.
It is the grace of the One who is strong enough to save.
Moses could see the Promised Land from a distance.
But in Christ, the promise of salvation is not something we merely admire from afar.
Through repentance and faith, we are invited to come to Him.
To receive forgiveness.
To walk in newness of life.
To live in the hope of the resurrection.
To trust the One who has gone before us.
And when the day comes that our own physical strength finally ends, our hope will not rest in how many years we lived, how much work we accomplished, or how many people applauded our names.
Our hope will rest in the crucified and risen Lord.
The One who saves.
The One who restores.
The One who keeps His promises.
The One who is worthy of our lives.
Moses died with strength still in his body, but the greatest hope of his story was never the strength he had left. It was the Savior who was still to come.
